title: How Nigerians Abroad Can Invest in NGX Stocks
summary: A clear guide for the diaspora on investing in Nigerian stocks: the CSCS account, the bank requirement, the CCI, and how to move money in and out.
body_markdown:
**In short:** Yes, Nigerians abroad can invest in NGX shares. You need a Bank Verification Number, which you can now get remotely, and a Non-Resident Nigerian account. With those, you can register on Bamboo and it opens your CSCS account for you. Returns are in naira, so currency movements affect their value.


If you are a Nigerian living abroad and have thought about[investing in the Nigerian market](https://investbamboo.com/nigerian-stocks) , you have probably hit the same wall most of the diaspora hits. The interest is there. What stops people is not desire but process: which accounts you need, whether you have to fly home to open them, and the quiet fear of putting money into Nigeria and not being able to get it back out.


The good news is that the process has become noticeably clearer over the past year. This guide walks you through how a Nigerian living abroad can invest in shares listed on the Nigerian Exchange (NGX), what accounts you need, how to set them up remotely, and what to understand about moving money in and out. Where the rules are technical, we point you to the right place rather than guess.


If you are new to the NGX and want the fundamentals first, start with our complete[guide to investing in the Nigerian stock market](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-to-invest-in-the-nigerian-stock-market-ngx-a-complete-beginners-guide/) , then come back here for the diaspora-specific steps.


## **Can you invest in the NGX from abroad?**


Yes. Nigerians in the diaspora can invest in shares listed on the NGX, and recent regulatory changes have made it more straightforward to do so without travelling back to Nigeria.


The route is different from simply downloading an app the way a resident might. As a non-resident, you work through a dedicated set of accounts designed for the diaspora, plus a licensed Nigerian stockbroker. The pieces are explained below, but the headline is simple: this is doable from your living room in London, Toronto, or Houston, and it no longer requires the trips and paperwork it once did.


## **Why the diaspora invests in the home market**


Investing in the NGX gives you a direct stake in Nigerian companies, in naira, alongside whatever you hold in your country of residence. For many in the diaspora, that is the appeal: exposure to the home economy, ownership in familiar names across banking, telecoms, and consumer goods, and dividends from companies that pay them.


The NGX is the[largest stock exchange in West Africa](https://www.mansamarkets.com/blog/african-stock-markets-complete-guide) , well ahead of its regional neighbours, so the range of companies to choose from is broad.


It is worth being clear-eyed, as with any market. Returns are never guaranteed, share prices can fall as well as rise, and you may get back less than you invest. For a diaspora investor there is an added layer, currency risk, which we cover further down. None of this is a reason not to invest. It is a reason to invest with your eyes open.


## **What you need: the three building blocks**


To invest in the NGX from abroad, you generally need three things: a Non-Resident Nigerian account that can hold and invest funds, a Bank Verification Number obtained remotely, and a CSCS account opened through a licensed stockbroker. Each is covered below.


## **The Non-Resident Nigerian accounts (NRNOA and NRNIA)**


In January 2025, the Central Bank of Nigeria introduced two dedicated accounts for Nigerians living abroad, and one of them is built specifically for investing. The[Central Bank’s framework](https://www.thecable.ng/cbn-launches-non-resident-account-for-nigerians-in-diaspora-to-invest-in-local-assets/) created the Non-Resident Nigerian Ordinary Account (NRNOA) and the Non-Resident Nigerian Investment Account (NRNIA).


The difference matters. The NRNOA is for remitting and managing your foreign earnings in Nigeria, in foreign currency or naira. The NRNIA is the one built for investing: it lets non-resident Nigerians put money into Nigerian assets, including instruments in the financial markets, in either foreign currency or naira.


A few important points from the[framework as analysed by legal commentators](https://www.banwo-ighodalo.com/grey-matter/understanding-cbns-dedicated-accounts-for-investment-and-management-of-remittances-by-nigerian-diaspora/) . These accounts are only for non-resident Nigerians. Nigerians living in Nigeria cannot open them. You can hold a foreign currency account, a naira account, or both. And opening one is subject to the know-your-customer checks the CBN requires.


For most diaspora investors who want NGX shares rather than just to send money home, the NRNIA is the account that matters.


## **The Non-Resident BVN (NRBVN)**


The single biggest change for the diaspora is that you can now get a Bank Verification Number remotely. In May 2025, the CBN and the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) launched the[Non-Resident BVN (NRBVN) platform](https://nibss-plc.com.ng/nrbvn/) , which lets Nigerians abroad enrol for a BVN without travelling home. You register on the platform, submit your ID and supporting documents, and complete a liveness check that verifies your identity digitally.


This sounds like a small administrative detail. It is not. The BVN requirement, and the old need to appear in person to satisfy it, was one of the main reasons diaspora investing stalled before people even began. Remote enrolment is what makes the rest of this process possible from abroad.


## **The CSCS account**


To hold Nigerian shares, you need a CSCS account, and you cannot open one directly as an individual. The Central Securities Clearing System (CSCS) is the depository that keeps the record of the shares you own. You get a CSCS account through a SEC-licensed Nigerian stockbroker, who opens it as part of bringing you on board.


This is where a platform like[Bamboo](https://investbamboo.com/) comes in. Bamboo is a SEC-registered Nigerian investing platform, and as a non-resident you can register on it once you have your BVN and a Non-Resident Nigerian account. It opens your CSCS account for you automatically, so there is no separate brokerage paperwork. The shares you buy are recorded against that account, the same as for any other NGX investor.


## **Moving your money in and out**


Yes, you can move your money back out of Nigeria, and the instrument that makes that possible is the Certificate of Capital Importation.


A Certificate of Capital Importation (CCI) is a document your Nigerian bank issues on behalf of the CBN, confirming that you brought foreign capital into the country for investment. As[Nigerian legal commentators explain](https://pavestoneslegal.com/doing-business-in-nigeria-the-relevance-of-the-certificate-of-capital-importation-to-foreign-investors-in-nigeria/) , it is the CCI that gives a foreign investor the right to repatriate capital, dividends, and profits at official foreign exchange rates in a convertible currency, after applicable taxes are paid. Without one, you would not be able to use the official market to take your money out.


In practice, that means a few things. Make sure a CCI is created when your funds come in, because it is difficult to claim repatriation rights later without it. Keep your tax affairs in order, since a tax clearance and payment of the dividend withholding tax are part of the process. And expect to route the repatriation through the same authorised bank, with the supporting documentation. The CBN has moved to electronic CCIs to make this smoother.


The Non-Resident Nigerian Investment Account framework is designed to sit alongside this and make capital mobility easier for the diaspora. Because these rules are set by the authorities and can change, confirm the current requirements with your bank before you invest rather than relying on a guide.


## **Step by step: how to start from abroad**


Here is the sequence at a high level. Confirm the specifics with your chosen platform or broker, since onboarding details differ.


1. **Get your Non-Resident BVN.** Obtain your NRBVN remotely through the designated platform, so your identity is verified without a trip to Nigeria.
2. **Open a Non-Resident Nigerian account.** Open an NRNIA (and an NRNOA if you also want to remit and manage funds), holding foreign currency, naira, or both, and complete the KYC the bank requires.
3. **Register on Bamboo.** With your BVN and Non-Resident Nigerian account (or a regular Nigerian Bank account) in place, register on Bamboo and activate your Nigerian stocks brokerage account. It opens your CSCS account automatically, so there is no separate brokerage paperwork.
4. **Fund your account.** Move money in through your Non-Resident Nigerian account. Use only official channels and verified account details. If anyone asks you to send money to a personal account, it is a scam.
5. **Invest.** Choose your shares, review the price, and buy. Your holdings are recorded against your CSCS account.


## **Tax for diaspora investors**


Dividends from Nigerian shares are subject to a withholding tax, and your wider tax position depends on where you live, so this needs care rather than a quick summary.


In Nigeria, a withholding tax applies to dividends, and it is reduced for investors from countries that have a tax treaty with Nigeria. On top of that, you may have tax obligations in your country of residence. Investors who are US persons, for example, have additional reporting requirements. Because this depends entirely on your personal circumstances, we cover Nigerian tax in detail in our guide to[tax on Nigerian stocks](https://learn.investbamboo.com/tax-on-nigerian-stocks-what-ngx-investors-need-to-know/) , and for your residence-country position you should speak to a qualified tax professional.


## **Risks to understand**


Investing in the NGX carries the normal risks of any stock market, plus one that matters more for the diaspora.


Share prices move, sometimes sharply, so the value of your holdings will rise and fall. Some stocks are thinly traded, which can make them harder to sell quickly at the price you want. And because your investments are in naira, the exchange rate between the naira and your home currency affects the real value of what you hold and what you eventually take out. A gain in naira can be reduced, erased, or magnified by currency movements by the time you convert it back. This currency risk cuts both ways, and it is the single most important thing for a diaspora investor to sit with before committing money. See[how naira movements affect your investments](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-naira-devaluation-and-inflation-affect-your-investments/) here.


As always, invest for the long term, spread your money rather than concentrating it, and only commit what you can afford to lose.


## **Frequently asked questions**


**Can a Nigerian living abroad invest in the NGX?** Yes. Non-resident Nigerians can invest in NGX-listed shares using a Non-Resident Nigerian Investment Account and a CSCS account opened through a licensed stockbroker. Recent changes, including the remote Non-Resident BVN, have made this possible without travelling to Nigeria.


**Do I need to travel to Nigeria to start?** No. The Non-Resident BVN can be obtained remotely, and banks offer digital onboarding, so the accounts can be opened from abroad.


**What is the difference between the NRNOA and the NRNIA?** The NRNOA is for remitting and managing your foreign earnings in Nigeria. The NRNIA is for investing in Nigerian assets. If your goal is to buy NGX shares, the NRNIA is the relevant account.


**Can I take my money back out of Nigeria?** Yes. Provided you brought your money in with a Certificate of Capital Importation, you have the right to repatriate your capital, dividends, and profits at official exchange rates, after applicable taxes. Confirm the current process with your bank, since these rules are set by the authorities and can change.


**Do diaspora investors pay tax on Nigerian shares?** Dividends are subject to a Nigerian withholding tax, reduced for investors from treaty countries. You may also have tax obligations where you live. Speak to a tax professional about your specific situation.

Past performance is not a reliable indicator of future results, and dividends are not guaranteed. Account, tax, and repatriation rules for non-resident Nigerians are set by the relevant authorities and can change. Before investing, consider your own circumstances and, if you are unsure, seek advice from a qualified professional.

### Quick Summary


This guide explains how Nigerians in the diaspora can invest in NGX-listed shares from abroad. Non-resident Nigerians can invest using a Non-Resident Nigerian account (the NRNIA for investing) and a Bank Verification Number, which can now be obtained remotely through the Non-Resident BVN platform launched by the CBN and NIBSS in 2025, without travelling to Nigeria. With a BVN and a Non-Resident Nigerian account, you can register on Bamboo, which opens your CSCS account automatically. Repatriation of capital, dividends, and profits is supported through a Certificate of Capital Importation, subject to applicable taxes.
